strengths: REFINE is a simple, intuitive, and modular ensemble active-learning method: repeated union-based filtering preserves candidates favored by complementary strategies, while the final coverage stage promotes batch diversity.

The empirical scope is strong for this setting, covering five held-out image datasets, three substantially different frozen foundation-model backbones, 20 acquisition cycles, and 10 trials. The appendix supplies complete learning curves rather than only selected results.

The reported results are consistently favorable. REFINE has 80–85% pairwise win rates against strong individual methods such as UHerding and BAIT, and 98–100% against the evaluated ensemble baselines. The full curves generally support these aggregate claims.

The ablations provide useful evidence that filtering itself matters: random sampling and several individual strategies improve when applied to the refined pool, sensitivity to R, alpha, and J is examined, and the Margin/TypiClust experiment illustrates how complementary notions of value can coexist in the candidate pool.

The method is practically attractive because it can wrap existing batch-selection strategies without retraining a policy or requiring task-specific knowledge of which strategy will work best. The paper is generally clear, well organized, and candid about sensitivity to poor or correlated ensemble members.
weaknesses: Theorem 3 is not established by its proof and appears false under the stated assumptions. For a random candidate set, the expected sample mean is generally E[(sum_x I_x V(x))/(sum_x I_x)], not the ratio (sum_x V(x)P_r(x))/(sum_x P_r(x)) used in the proof. Marginal survival probabilities that increase with value do not suffice when the selected-set size is random and inclusion events are dependent. A fixed-size or stronger joint-inclusion assumption would be needed. Consequently, the claimed monotonic guarantee on candidate-pool value should not be presented as proven.

The statistical reporting is inadequate relative to the strength of the empirical claims. Standard errors are explicitly omitted, no confidence intervals or significance tests are supplied, and numerical AULC means and dispersion are absent. Pairwise trial-level win rates are useful but do not reveal effect sizes or uncertainty, especially where learning curves are close.

REFINE uses up to M×J strategy executions in each of R rounds—nominally 8×10×5 proposal calls per acquisition cycle—plus final UHerding selection. No measured runtime, memory usage, candidate-pool sizes, or compute-matched comparison is reported. Thus the claim that the overhead is a reasonable practical tradeoff is unsupported, and some gains may reflect substantially greater selection computation than the baselines receive.

The ablations do not fully isolate the proposed design. There is no direct comparison against simpler matched-compute alternatives such as a one-shot union followed by the same coverage selector, repeated execution of only UHerding, or random candidate pools matched in size. Table 2 studies random downstream sampling, but it does not quantify how progressive depth affects the complete REFINE pipeline.

Reproducibility is limited: the manuscript contains only an anonymous code placeholder and promises release after acceptance. It also omits the hyperparameter-search grid and selection criterion, detailed dataset split protocols for several datasets, baseline-specific settings, and measured refined-pool sizes. The ESC50 use case uses a random 20% split without reported repetitions and focuses on a single failing downstream strategy, so it provides only illustrative evidence.

The claimed breadth should be interpreted carefully: CIFAR-10 is used for hyperparameter selection, leaving five image datasets as held-out evaluations; all main experiments freeze the representation and train only a linear head. The evidence therefore does not establish behavior under end-to-end fine-tuning or representation shift during active learning. Overall, the promising and consistent empirical contribution is balanced by a materially invalid theoretical claim and incomplete statistical and computational validation.

strengths: REFINE is a simple, intuitive ensemble approach: repeated union-based filtering preserves candidates favored by complementary active-learning strategies, followed by coverage-based batch selection.

The main evaluation is broad within frozen-feature image classification: five held-out datasets, three foundation-model backbones, eight individual baselines, three ensemble baselines, and ten trials. The reported learning curves show sizable and generally consistent improvements.

The ablations examine filtering depth, subsampling ratio, number of proposed batches, downstream selectors, and complementary uncertainty/representativeness strategies. Hyperparameters are selected on CIFAR-10 and the principal claims are evaluated on other datasets.
The paper is clearly organized, gives pseudocode and complexity expressions, acknowledges sensitivity to weak or correlated ensemble members, and includes a useful audio-domain case study.
weaknesses: Theorem 3 is not established by its proof. The candidate pool is random, but the proof equates its expected sample mean with a ratio of marginal expected totals; in general, the expectation of a random ratio is not the ratio of expectations. Dependence among inclusions is also ignored. Moreover, assuming every constituent strategy orders every pair consistently with the same unknown true value is exceptionally strong and conflicts with the paper's motivation that strategies capture different notions of value. Thus, the claimed guarantee of monotonically increasing pool value is unsupported.

The statistical reporting is inadequate for the central empirical claims. Standard errors are explicitly omitted, no numerical per-dataset AULC means or variances are supplied, and no paired statistical analysis is reported. Pooled win rates over heterogeneous datasets, backbones, and trials do not reveal effect uncertainty or dependence. Consequently, claims such as consistent superiority and 100% win rates are harder to assess than the extensive experiment count suggests.

The comparison does not account for the method's very large selection-time budget. With R=5, J=10, and all eight individual baselines in the ensemble, REFINE can invoke component selectors hundreds of times per active-learning cycle before its final UHerding step. There are no wall-clock, memory, candidate-pool-size, or compute-matched comparisons, despite claims of computational practicality and efficiency. Parallelization changes resource requirements rather than eliminating this cost.

The empirical advantage cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed progressive mechanism. REFINE aggregates every individual baseline and then applies a strong baseline, UHerding, again for final selection. Missing ablations include a one-round union with matched proposal count/compute, random repeated filtering with matched pool sizes, alternative ensemble subsets, leave-one-strategy-out tests, and direct separation of progressive filtering from the benefit of substantially more selector evaluations.

Reproducibility is limited: code is deferred until acceptance, while important implementation information such as baseline-specific hyperparameters, exact data splits, kernel and uncertainty-weight details, validation procedure, and computational resources is absent. The audio result uses only one random 80/20 split and provides no uncertainty estimate.

The repeated filtering-and-union idea is useful but technically modest, and the stated theoretical contribution does not currently provide sound justification. Considering the invalid central guarantee, uncontrolled compute advantage, and insufficient uncertainty reporting together, the evidence does not yet support acceptance despite promising empirical trends.

strengths: REFINE is a simple, original, and practically useful ensemble active-learning framework: iterative union-based filtering preserves candidates favored by complementary strategies, while coverage-based selection produces the final batch.

The empirical evaluation is broad and generally convincing, covering five held-out image datasets, three substantially different foundation-model backbones, 20 acquisition cycles, and 10 independent trials. REFINE consistently outperforms both individual strategies and three prior ensemble methods, often throughout the learning curve rather than only at a single budget.

The ablations provide useful evidence for the central mechanism. Random sampling and several individual strategies improve when applied to the filtered pool; performance is reasonably robust to the filtering hyperparameters; and the Margin/TypiClust experiment illustrates how complementary uncertainty and representativeness signals can coexist in the candidate pool.

The ESC50 audio-spectrogram study suggests that progressive filtering transfers beyond the principal image benchmarks and can improve a downstream strategy that is not itself included in the filtering ensemble.

The paper is well organized, clearly motivates its design choices, supplies full learning curves in the supplement, and candidly discusses degradation when the ensemble contains poorly performing or correlated strategies.
weaknesses: Theorem 3 is not established by the provided proof. For a random candidate set, the expected sample average is generally not equal to the ratio of expected value mass to expected cardinality used in Step 3. Additional assumptions and a correct treatment of the random denominator are required. Moreover, assuming that every constituent strategy is monotone in one common, unknown 'true value' is very strong and sits uneasily with the paper's motivation that strategies capture different notions of value. Thus, the theoretical contribution is weaker than claimed, although the empirical contribution remains intact.

Statistical reporting is insufficient for such a stochastic evaluation. Despite running 10 trials, the paper omits standard errors from all curves and provides neither numerical mean AULCs with uncertainty nor paired significance/confidence analyses. Aggregated win rates conceal effect sizes and heterogeneity across dataset-backbone combinations; the full curves visually support the claims, but their reliability cannot be assessed precisely.

REFINE is potentially expensive: with the stated defaults it invokes each of eight strategies across 10 subsamples and five rounds per acquisition cycle, followed by UHerding. The paper gives asymptotic discussion but no wall-clock, memory, candidate-pool-size, or compute-normalized comparison. The parallelization argument also presumes substantial hardware. This materially limits assessment of the claimed practical efficiency.

The component analysis is incomplete. There is no systematic leave-one-strategy-out or strategy-composition study, no direct comparison against simple score/rank aggregation or a one-round union at matched compute, and limited isolation of the benefit due specifically to the final UHerding stage. Such comparisons would clarify which complexity is necessary and whether gains depend on including strong methods such as UHerding in both filtering and final selection.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the manuscript does not fully specify dataset splits and preprocessing, baseline-specific hyperparameters, whether classifier heads are reinitialized or warm-started each cycle, handling when a sampled intermediate pool contains fewer than one batch, or whether initial pools and training randomness are paired across methods. The code is only promised after acceptance.

Some claims are broader than the evidence. The assertion that filtering improves 'any' strategy is supported for a finite collection, chiefly on CIFAR-100 plus one ESC50 case, and random subsampling provides opportunities to inspect the full pool but does not guarantee that the entire pool is explored. These are presentation-level overstatements rather than failures of the demonstrated method.

strengths: REFINE is a simple, original, and practically useful ensemble active-learning framework: repeated union-based filtering preserves candidates favored by complementary strategies, while coverage-based selection produces the annotation batch.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for active learning, covering five held-out image datasets, three distinct foundation backbones, 20 acquisition cycles, and 10 independent trials, with comparisons against eight individual and four ensemble baselines.

The evidence consistently favors REFINE across most dataset-backbone combinations, including both absolute and relative learning curves. The paper also reports uncertainty, pairwise win rates, corrected statistical tests, class-imbalance and distribution-shift experiments, partial fine-tuning, and an audio-domain use case.

The ablations meaningfully examine filtering depth, subsampling ratio, number of proposed batches, batch size, weak ensemble members, alternative second-stage selectors, and applying several downstream strategies to the filtered pool. These results support progressive filtering as the main source of improvement rather than only the chosen final selector.
The manuscript is clear and candid about an important limitation: performance can deteriorate when the ensemble is dominated by weak or correlated strategies.
weaknesses: Theorem 3 is not established by its proof. The expected average value of a random set is E[(sum_x V(x) I_x)/(sum_x I_x)], which generally is not the ratio of expected sums used in the appendix. Monotone marginal survival probabilities alone are also insufficient under correlated batch-selection events. Thus, the claimed guarantee of monotonically increasing expected pool value requires stronger assumptions or a different argument.

The theoretical results otherwise provide limited explanatory force. Theorems 1 and 2 largely follow from the definitions of valuable and uninformative instances and assume independent repeated draws, while Theorem 3 assumes every constituent strategy ranks all instances consistently with an unknown true value—precisely the property that often fails and motivates an ensemble.

The gains come at substantial acquisition cost: with the reported defaults, every cycle invokes each ensemble strategy J=10 times over R=5 rounds before another selection stage. Sequential acquisition is around ten minutes in the reported example. The much lower parallel times are projections based on assumed parallel fractions and scheduling overhead, not measurements, and require up to 80 processes. Comparisons therefore establish label efficiency more strongly than practical compute efficiency.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: the implementation URL is blank, the exact default membership of the strategy set S is not stated in one explicit location, and several operational details—minimum-pool enforcement, random seeds, dataset splits, kernel and UHerding settings—are deferred or insufficiently specified.

Some claims are broader than the evidence. The statement that filtering benefits 'any' strategy is based mainly on five strategies on CIFAR-100 with two backbones plus one Coreset audio study; the claim of robustness to out-of-distribution data uses only two small MedMNIST datasets. These are promising findings but not universal validation.

The statistical significance statement uses 18 dataset-model blocks, apparently including CIFAR-10 even though it was used for hyperparameter selection and excluded from the stated main evaluation. Reporting the held-out-only analysis would better align the test with the experimental protocol.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for active learning: five held-out image datasets, three pretrained backbones, ten trials, eight individual strategies, and four ensemble baselines. The paper includes useful stress tests beyond the main benchmark, including class imbalance, distribution shift, partial backbone fine-tuning, varying batch size, weak ensemble members, and an audio-spectrogram use case.

The ablations isolate progressive filtering from the final selector: random sampling and several individual strategies improve when applied to the filtered pool, providing evidence that the first stage contributes beyond merely wrapping UHerding.
The manuscript is clearly organized, provides pseudocode, reports standard errors, and explicitly acknowledges sensitivity to the quality and composition of the strategy ensemble.
weaknesses: Material: Theorem 3 is not established by its proof. Step 3 replaces the expectation of the random pool average, E[(sum_x V(x)I_x)/(sum_x I_x)], with the ratio of expected numerator and denominator, (sum_x V(x)P_r(x))/(sum_x P_r(x)). These quantities are not equal in general because the selected pool size and composition are random and dependent. Consequently, the claimed monotonic guarantee on expected candidate-pool value does not follow.

Material: The other theoretical results offer limited explanatory support. Theorems 1 and 2 largely restate repeated-selection probabilities after defining a valuable or uninformative point through its probability of being selected. Theorem 3 additionally assumes every ensemble strategy orders every pair consistently with the same unknown 'true value,' which conflicts with the paper's motivation of complementary notions of value and with its observed weak strategies. Thus, the manuscript overstates the strength of its theoretical analysis.

Material: The accuracy gains come with a very large and unequal acquisition budget: the default procedure invokes each of eight strategies for 10 batches over five rounds, followed by UHerding. Table 3 reports roughly ten minutes of sequential acquisition per cycle and only projected—not measured—parallel times using as many as 80 processes. Comparisons against single-strategy baselines therefore do not establish performance at comparable computation, memory, or hardware budgets, limiting the practical usefulness claim.

Material: REFINE includes UHerding as both an ensemble contributor and the final selector, while being compared directly with a single application of UHerding. Although the filtering ablations show added value, there is no compute-matched control such as repeated UHerding, repeated subsampling with one strategy, or an ensemble with an equal number of acquisition calls. It remains unclear how much improvement comes from the proposed cross-strategy mechanism versus substantially more stochastic search.

Material: Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript. The sentence 'Our implementation can be found at' has no URL, and several consequential details are missing or deferred to unavailable code, including preprocessing/augmentation, exact strategy-specific settings, the operational rule when a subsample becomes smaller than the requested batch, and sufficient detail to reproduce the projected runtime calculation.

The evaluation is strong but not entirely cleanly separated from model selection. CIFAR-10 is used to tune R, J, and alpha, yet it is later included among the 18 dataset-by-model blocks used for the global significance claim. The paper should report the statistical conclusion on the 15 held-out blocks alone and provide corrected p-values or effect sizes, rather than only stating significance at 0.01.

Presentation refinement: Some claims are broader than the evidence, including that filtering improves 'any' active-learning strategy and that REFINE is the 'first' ensemble method to consistently surpass individual baselines. The experiments support the tested strategies and configurations, not universal or priority claims. Overall, the extensive positive results keep the paper near the decision boundary, but the invalid central theorem and unresolved compute-matched attribution prevent a confident acceptance recommendation.

strengths: REFINE offers a simple, original, and practically useful formulation of ensemble active learning: progressively retaining the union of candidates proposed by complementary strategies, followed by coverage-based batch selection. The separation between identifying valuable candidates and ensuring batch coverage is intuitive and technically well motivated.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad for active learning. It covers six image datasets, three pretrained vision backbones, eight individual strategies, four ensemble baselines, 20 acquisition cycles, and 10 trials. The supplementary experiments further examine class imbalance, out-of-distribution medical data, partial backbone fine-tuning, alternative batch sizes, and an audio application.

The reported results strongly support the central empirical claim. REFINE has high pairwise AULC win rates against strong individual methods such as BAIT and UHerding and wins nearly all comparisons against prior ensemble methods. Complete absolute and relative learning curves are supplied rather than only selected endpoint results.

The ablations isolate several important components: filtering depth, subsampling ratio, number of proposed batches, filtering as preprocessing for different downstream selectors, and an ensemble restricted to two complementary strategies. In particular, improvements obtained even when randomly sampling from the refined pool provide persuasive evidence that progressive filtering improves candidate-pool quality.

Hyperparameters are selected on CIFAR-10 and transferred to the other main datasets, reducing dataset-specific tuning concerns. The authors also acknowledge and experimentally illustrate a relevant failure mode when most ensemble members are weak.

The method is modular and can incorporate new selection strategies. Its demonstrated use as preprocessing for a strategy outside the filtering ensemble, including the separate audio experiment, increases its potential usefulness beyond the exact REFINE configuration.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is substantially weaker than its presentation suggests. Theorem 3 assumes that every constituent strategy ranks every pair of instances monotonically according to the same unknown true value in every round. This is an exceptionally strong condition that conflicts with the paper's motivation that strategies encode different, sometimes competing notions of value. Consequently, the theorem provides little explanation for REFINE in the intended setting.

The proof of Theorem 3 equates the expected average value of a random, variable-size union with a ratio of inclusion-probability-weighted sums. In general, the expectation of a random ratio is not the ratio of expectations; additional fixed-cardinality or sampling assumptions would be required. Thus the stated monotonicity result is not established as written. Theorems 1 and 2 are more elementary survival bounds and rely on independence assumptions that should be stated explicitly.

REFINE uses up to R×J×M strategy executions per acquisition cycle, making its computational budget far larger than that of a single-strategy baseline. The reported sequential timings help, but the large parallel speedups are projections based on assumed parallel fractions and as many as 80 processes rather than measured executions. A clearer compute-normalized comparison and measured parallel runtime would be important for judging practical efficiency.

The evidence is presented mainly through learning curves and pairwise win proportions. These summaries obscure effect sizes for individual dataset-backbone combinations. A numerical AULC table with uncertainty, per-task differences, and exact corrected statistical results would make it easier to assess whether the many wins are consistently meaningful rather than sometimes very small.

The statistical analysis pools 18 dataset-model blocks, apparently including CIFAR-10 even though it was used for hyperparameter selection. That tuned dataset should be excluded from confirmatory significance testing or reported separately. Statistical significance is stated only broadly, without test statistics, adjusted p-values, or confidence intervals.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the implementation sentence contains no actual link, and important details such as preprocessing/augmentation, exact splits and seeds, strategy-specific hyperparameters, and the precise ensemble configuration are not fully consolidated. These are presentation and documentation issues rather than evidence that the empirical results are invalid, but they prevent straightforward independent reproduction.

Some claims are broader than the experiments warrant. For example, the manuscript says filtering improves 'any' individual strategy, while only a finite subset is tested, and calls the method state of the art despite one documented degradation and without a compute-matched evaluation. These claims should be narrowed to the demonstrated settings.
